examples.problem_statement: 15 men could finish a piece of work in 210 days. But at the end of 100 days, 15 additional men are employed. In how many more days will the work be complete?

solution.description: Convert the whole job into man-days by multiplying the original 15 men by the 210 days they would have needed.
Measure the work finished in the first phase: 15 men worked for the first 100 days.
Subtract the man-days already spent from the total man-days to get the work still outstanding.
Divide the remaining man-days by the new daily strength of 30 men (the original 15 plus the 15 additional men) to get the number of further days needed.

key_reminders: Total work can be expressed as (number of men) \times (number of days) in man-days.
Man-days already spent are subtracted from total man-days to get work remaining.
Days remaining = work remaining in man-days divided by the men now working each day.
common_mistakes: Dividing the remaining 1650 man-days by 15 instead of by the enlarged workforce of 30.
Reporting the total elapsed time rather than the additional days asked for.

examples.problem_statement: After the US Civil War, “carpetbaggers”—so-called because they carried suitcases made of inexpensive carpeting material— _________ the South, hoping to turn a quick profit.

solution.operation: Fill the blank with your own words before looking at the choices: “went to”
solution.result: A working prediction of movement into the South
solution.description: Read the sentence and supply your own filler for the blank, so the answer choices are judged against your prediction rather than against each other.

solution.operation: Locate the clue: the carpetbaggers carried suitcases
solution.description: Identify the detail in the sentence that supports the prediction — people carrying suitcases were probably on the move.
Strike out each option that introduces an idea the sentence never indicates, since none of conquering, blacklisting, boycotting or scolding is supported here.

solution.operation: Check the survivor: inundated = flooded, overwhelmed
solution.description: Confirm the one remaining choice by substituting its meaning back into the sentence, where flooding into the South matches the prediction.

key_reminders: Predict a filler for the blank from the sentence itself before reading the options.
The clue for the blank is stated in the sentence — here, the suitcases.
Reject any choice that adds an idea the sentence does not indicate.
common_mistakes: Picking a hostile-sounding word such as vanquished or berated because the passage's subject feels negative, though the sentence itself indicates only arrival.

examples.problem_statement: A boy buys oranges at 9 for Rs 16 and sells them at 11 for Rs 20. What does he gain or lose per cent?

solution.result: A quantity divisible by both 9 and 11
solution.description: Choose 99 as the working number of oranges so that both the buying lot of 9 and the selling lot of 11 divide it exactly and no fractions appear.
Scale the buying rate of Rs 16 per 9 oranges up to 99 oranges to get the total cost price.
Scale the selling rate of Rs 20 per 11 oranges up to the same 99 oranges to get the total selling price.

solution.result: Profit of Rs 4 on a cost of Rs 176
solution.description: Subtract cost price from selling price to get the absolute profit on the 99 oranges.
Express the profit as a percentage of the cost price, which is the base for gain per cent.

solution.result: Same 2 3/11 per cent, positive so it is a gain
solution.description: Apply the book's quicker cross method directly to the four given numbers, cross-multiplying the rates and dividing by the cost cross-product; the positive sign marks it a gain.

key_reminders: Work with a quantity that is a common multiple of the buying and selling lot sizes.
Gain per cent is computed on the cost price, not the selling price.
Cross method: profit per cent = (buy-quantity \times sell-price - buy-price \times sell-quantity) / (buy-price \times sell-quantity) \times 100, positive meaning gain.
common_mistakes: Comparing the rates Rs 16 and Rs 20 directly without equalising the number of oranges (9 versus 11).
Dividing the Rs 4 profit by the selling price 180 instead of the cost price 176.

concept.technique_name: linear equation from a divide-instead-of-multiply error

examples.problem_statement: A boy was asked to find 7/9 of a fraction. He made a mistake of dividing the fraction by 7/9 and so got an answer which exceeded the correct answer by 8/21. Find the correct answer.

solution.operation: Let the fraction be x; \frac{x}{7/9} - x \times \frac{7}{9} = \frac{8}{21}
solution.description: Name the unknown fraction x and set the wrong result (x divided by 7/9) minus the correct result (7/9 of x) equal to the stated excess of 8/21.

solution.result: Both terms written with x as a coefficient
solution.description: Rewrite the division by 7/9 as multiplication by 9/7 so the left side is two like terms in x.
Combine the two terms over the common denominator 63, subtracting the numerators 81 and 49 to leave 32.
Solve for x by multiplying both sides by the reciprocal of the coefficient 32/63, giving the original fraction.
Take 7/9 of the recovered fraction, which is what the question originally asked for, to get the correct answer.

key_reminders: Dividing by 7/9 is the same as multiplying by 9/7.
“Of” means multiply, so the correct answer is 7/9 \times x.
The question asks for the correct answer, not the fraction x itself — one further multiplication is needed after solving.
common_mistakes: Stopping at x = 3/4 and reporting it instead of taking 7/9 of it.
Reversing the difference and writing the correct answer minus the wrong one, since 9x/7 is the larger of the two.

concept.technique_name: constant percentage profit implies income proportional to expenditure

examples.problem_statement:
Refer to the line chart of percentage profit earned by companies A and B over the years 2003-2008 (B: 2003 = 30, 2004 = 60, 2005 = 80, 2006 = 80, 2007 = 70, 2008 = 100). If the expenditure of company B increases by 20% from 2005 to 2006, the income in 2006 will be how many times the income in 2005?
(a) 2.16 times (b) 1.2 times (c) 1.8 times (d) None of these

solution.operation: Read company B's percentage profit for 2005 and 2006 from the chart
solution.result: Both years show the same percentage profit
solution.description: Compare B's two plotted points on the chart and note that the profit percentage does not change between 2005 and 2006.

solution.operation: Equal profit per cent \Rightarrow income rises in the same proportion as expenditure, i.e. by 20\%
solution.result: Income in 2006 is 120 for every 100 in 2005
solution.description: Since profit per cent is fixed, income is a fixed multiple of expenditure, so a 20% rise in expenditure carries a 20% rise in income.
Form the ratio of the 2006 income to the 2005 income from those proportional figures to get how many times larger it is.

key_reminders: Percentage profit = (income - expenditure) / expenditure \times 100, so a constant profit per cent fixes the income-to-expenditure ratio.
When that ratio is fixed, income scales by exactly the same percentage as expenditure.
common_mistakes: Combining the 20% expenditure rise with the 80% profit figure (e.g. 1.2 \times 1.8 = 2.16) even though the profit per cent is unchanged between the two years.
